entries.caption:
Kimi K3 on 8GB RAM, no GPU: a 2.78T AI model runs locally. The catch is your disk.

RAM peaked at 8.24 GB (a server with its RAM capped at 8 GB), and the output was byte-identical from 8 GB to 224 GB: more RAM changes the speed, not the answer.

Kimi K3 hardware requirements, the honest version:
- about 1.7 TB free on a fast SSD
- hours of download (about 3.5 h at 1 Gbps)
- about 30 seconds per token on a fast server
- nearly 16 minutes for one word on an 8 GB Jetson board with a hard drive
- text only: a proof of concept, not an everyday app

Running an LLM locally without a GPU is possible. The memory wall just moved to your disk. Kimi K3 itself is open-weight under Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 License, free to download.

entries.caption:
Kimi K3 on 8 GB RAM with no GPU: a 2.78-trillion-parameter open-weight LLM ran locally, and the real hardware requirement is your disk, not your memory.
Free setup guide: https://withhammad.com/resources/kimi-k3-on-8gb-ram

How kimi-k3-in-c, an Apache-2.0 C engine by Fareed Khan, does it:
- About 93% of Moonshot AI's 1.56 TB checkpoint is mixture-of-experts weights.
- Those experts stay on a fast NVMe SSD, and each token reads only 16 of 896 experts per layer.
- Output is byte-identical from 8 GB to 224 GB of RAM. More memory changes the speed, not the answer.

What it really costs:
- About 1.7 TB of free disk before you download a single byte.
- Hours of downloading (about 3.5 hours at 1 Gbps).
- About 30 seconds per token, measured on a 124-core server with its RAM capped at 8 GB.
- On an 8 GB Jetson board with a hard drive, one word ("Paris") took nearly 16 minutes.

So treat it as a proof of concept, not an everyday app: text only, no server, no quality benchmark.

For UAE businesses that handle client data, the interesting part is privacy. A model you run locally keeps prompts on your own machine; a hosted API sends them to another company's servers. The memory wall did not disappear. It moved to your disk.

Kimi K3 is open weights under Moonshot's own Kimi K3 License, a custom license rather than an OSI open-source one. The engine is Apache-2.0.

entries.caption:
How to track AI referral traffic in GA4, and whether AI search visitors really convert better. One Semrush study found them 4.4x as valuable as organic search visitors, by conversion rate.
Free setup guide: https://withhammad.com/resources/ai-traffic-ga4

Why it can happen: people research inside ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini before they click, so they arrive further down the funnel than someone scanning search results.

The stat, honestly: Semrush (Jul 2025) measured the average AI search visitor at 4.4x the value of an organic search visitor, based on conversion rate. It is one vendor study with an undisclosed sample. Other studies range from about 1.3x to over 20x.

So measure your own AI traffic:

1. Check your AI visibility. Ask ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini the questions your customers ask. Are you mentioned, and described correctly?
2. Open GA4 > Reports > Acquisition > Traffic acquisition and find the AI Assistant channel (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, Grok and more).
3. Add "AI (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini)" to your "Where did you hear about us?" form.
4. Split those customers out and compare conversion rate and order value against search and social.

Two caveats: Google AI Overviews and AI Mode stay in Organic Search, not the AI Assistant channel. And many AI clicks arrive with no referrer and land in Direct, so the channel undercounts. A custom channel group can add sources like perplexity.ai and claude.ai; the full guide covers it: https://withhammad.com/resources/ai-traffic-ga4

entries.title: NVIDIA SkillSpector: scan Claude Code skills before you install them
entries.caption:
Claude Code security starts with the skills you install. NVIDIA SkillSpector is a free, open-source scanner that gives each skill a 0-100 risk score before it reaches your machine.
Free setup guide: https://withhammad.com/resources/skillspector-scan-skills

A Jan 2026 study of 31,132 marketplace agent skills (Liu et al.) found 26.1% had at least one vulnerability, and 5.2% showed high-severity patterns strongly suggesting malicious intent. Confirmed malicious skills are rarer (157 of 98,380 in a follow-up study, all removed), but one bad skill could still leak your API keys.

How to use NVIDIA SkillSpector:
1. Install it with uv from NVIDIA's GitHub: uv tool install git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git (on Python 3.14, add --python 3.12)
2. Scan a skill folder, GitHub link or zip. To check everything you already have: skillspector scan ~/.claude/skills --recursive --no-llm
3. Read the score: 0-20 low, 21-50 caution, over 50 do not install.
4. Keep --no-llm on for private or client skills, so the code stays on your machine.

It checks 17 risk categories, including prompt injection, data exfiltration, tool misuse and MCP tool poisoning. On its own test skills (Oct 2026), the safe one scored 0/100 and the malicious one 100/100.

The honest caveat: a low score means no red flags were found, not that a skill is proven safe. It is a scanner, not a sandbox, and it is not on PyPI, so install it only from NVIDIA's repo. Treat it as one layer of AI agent security, next to Anthropic's own advice to install skills only from sources you trust.

Full guide, no comment needed: https://withhammad.com/resources/skillspector-scan-skills

entries.caption:
Are Claude Code skills safe? Scan them with NVIDIA SkillSpector before you install.
Comment SCAN and I'll DM you the guide.

About 1 in 4 marketplace skills had a security flaw, and 5.2% showed strong signs of malicious intent (Liu et al., Jan 2026). One bad skill could leak your API keys.

NVIDIA SkillSpector is a free, open-source scanner (Apache-2.0). Feed it a skill folder, GitHub link or zip. It checks 17 risk categories, like prompt injection, data exfiltration and tool misuse, and gives a 0-100 risk score:
- 0-20: low risk
- 21-50: caution
- over 50: don't install

A low score means no red flags were found, not that a skill is proven safe. Use --no-llm to keep your code on your machine, or let Claude Code or Codex run it for you.

entries.title: How an AI agent works: one loop inside a harness
entries.caption:
How AI agents actually work: a model inside a harness runs one loop (build context, decide, act with tools, observe, repeat) until it answers or a step cap stops it.
Free guide (build your first small agent with Claude Code): https://withhammad.com/resources/how-ai-agents-work

1. Trigger: you, an event, a timer or another agent starts it
2. Build context: instructions, tool list, chat so far, recalled memory, earlier tool results
3. Model decides: answer now, or call a tool
4. Act: the harness runs the tool (search, code, files, APIs, MCP servers, sub-agents)
5. Observe: the result goes back into the context and the loop runs again
Around it all: memory, guardrails, permissions, human sign-off, observability and evals. The model only writes text; the harness does the rest.
Set a step cap: without one, a failing call can repeat and every try costs money.

Sources: ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629 and Anthropic, Building effective agents https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents

entries.title: How an AI agent works: one loop inside a harness
entries.caption:
How AI agents work: one loop inside a harness. Want to really understand AI agents? Don't just read about them. Build a small one.

First, here's what's going on inside, in plain words.

Most agents run the same loop (it has a name: ReAct): think, act, look at the result, go again.

Let's walk one request through it.
You type: "Move my 3pm with Omar to Thursday."

𝟭/ 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁
→ The model can't see your calendar. It only sees what the harness hands it.
→ Your message, its instructions, the tools it may use, anything pulled from memory.
→ If nothing says which Omar, it has to guess or ask.

𝟮/ 𝗗𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗲
→ It reads all of that and picks one next step: reply now, or use a tool.
→ Here it needs the calendar.
→ The model only writes text. It can't move a meeting on its own.

𝟯/ 𝗔𝗰𝘁
→ It writes a tool call: "find today's 15:00 event with Omar".
→ The harness runs that call against your calendar.
→ Get the date wrong in the call and it finds nothing.

𝟰/ 𝗢𝗯𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗲
→ The result comes back: "1 event found", or "no match".
→ The harness adds it to the context and asks the model again.
→ Now it decides: move it, ask you, or stop.

That loop repeats until the model says it's done or a limit stops it.
With no step cap, it can retry the same failing call again and again, and you pay for every one.

𝟱/ 𝗖𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗽
→ Permissions: what the agent may touch
→ Guardrails: what it must never do
→ Evals: whether its results are actually right
→ Human sign-off: who approves the risky actions
→ Traces and logs: what it did, and why

So understanding an agent means seeing what it was given, what it called, what came back, and who checked it.

Once you can see that, you can debug it and make it better.

Next step: build one. You'll learn more in an afternoon than in a month of reading.

entries.title: Harness engineering: the layer that makes an AI agent reliable
entries.caption:
Harness engineering: why AI agents fail in real work even when the model is fine.

When an agent breaks, people blame the model. Often the system around it is the problem.

Free guide, a checklist for each layer: https://withhammad.com/resources/harness-engineering

Everyone chases smarter agents:
A bigger model.
A better prompt.
More context.

The harness is everything around the model that keeps the agent dependable.

The model suggests what to do.
The harness decides how, and whether, it happens.

1/ Context Builder
→ The docs and data that matter
→ What's already been said and done
→ Where the task stands right now
Skip this and the model fills the gaps with guesses.

2/ The Model
It reasons, picks a tool, suggests an action.
It can also make things up, misread an instruction or loop on the same step.
A strong model helps. It doesn't make the result safe.

3/ Permission Check
→ May it read this data?
→ May it change this record?
→ Does a human need to sign off first?
That call belongs to your system, not the model.

4/ Tools & Runtime
APIs. Databases. CRMs. MCP servers.
Give each tool only the access the task needs. Then one wrong decision stays a small one.

5/ Verification
→ Did the payment really go through?
→ Is the right record updated?
→ Do the tests pass?
The model can say it worked. Your system has to show it.

6/ Observability & Feedback
Log every tool call. Record the errors. Count the retries.
Feed what you learn back into the system.
A failure you can see is a failure you can fix.

The short version: the model comes up with options. The harness turns them into actions, inside clear rules, and checks the result instead of trusting the reply.

That's the gap between a good demo and an AI product people can rely on.
